communicate-with-mastery-01: Before drafting, decide who your audience is and what you want them to do, then choose channel and structure.
communicate-with-mastery-02: After drafting, edit so the actor and real verb come first, filler is cut, and your point is easy to find.
communicate-with-mastery-03: Make sure a reader skimming only the subject line, headings, and first sentences still gets your point and request.
communicate-with-mastery-04: Report the fact, explain why it matters to this audience, then state the action or decision it calls for.
communicate-with-mastery-05: Open at the most interesting moment, then add only the context needed; save names and logistics for later.
communicate-with-mastery-06: When presenting, deliver one complete thought while looking at one person, then move to someone else for the next.
communicate-with-mastery-07: Know your end point, then shape the anecdote as normal situation, disruption, consequences, and what has changed now.
communicate-with-mastery-08: Share something personal only when it serves your point, and plan how you open and close so your message lasts.
communicate-with-mastery-09: Pause before you send or speak, check the receiver understood you, and use what you learn next time.
communicate-with-mastery-10: Stop chasing a perfect performance; review each important talk or message and set a few goals for next time.
communicate-with-mastery-11: Give each slide one message shown visually, design the talk first, and never end on a 'Questions?' slide.
communicate-with-mastery-12: In video and phone meetings, deliberately signal attention, manage turn-taking, and confirm understanding, since nonverbal cues are lost.
communicate-with-mastery-13: To add weight to a key moment, lower your pitch and slow down, and avoid rising intonation on statements.
communicate-with-mastery-14: Put your effort into being understood through pace, structure, and visuals, not into hiding who you are.
communicate-with-mastery-15: Coach by asking guiding questions instead of rewriting, then rehearse speakers together so they learn from each other's feedback.
communicate-with-mastery-16: For high-stakes messages, map audience, messenger, channels, resources, partners, structure, and desired results before you write.
communicate-with-mastery-17: Work separately on what you say, how it sounds, and what people see, and keep going calmly after a stumble.
communicate-with-mastery-18: Pitch the problem, your solution, the market, and the business, moving listeners from curious to understanding to evangelism.
communicate-with-mastery-19: Before speaking, tell yourself you are excited rather than nervous, and treat the talk more like a conversation.
communicate-with-mastery-20: Review your recording four times: once to get past cringing, sound only, picture only, then everything noting strengths.
connect-01: Move relationships toward being yourselves, mutually vulnerable, trusting, honest, handling conflict well, and committed to each other's growth.
connect-02: Deepen a relationship by sharing a little more than feels comfortable, then stretch further only if they reciprocate.
connect-03: Speak with authority about what someone did and how it affected you, but never claim to know their intentions.
connect-04: Give feedback by naming a specific behavior and its impact on you, without labels, motive guesses, or a praise sandwich.
connect-05: Raise small irritations early and without accusation, before silence turns them into a bigger, harder blowup.
connect-06: Name real feelings in one or two words instead of disguising judgments as 'I feel that you...'.
connect-07: Treat all feedback as useful data about how you land, even if you do not agree or act on it.
connect-08: Use feedback to open joint problem solving, expecting to learn missing context and that both sides may need to change.
connect-09: When someone brings a problem, ask open how, what, when, or where questions before offering advice, and avoid why.
connect-10: Stop managing your image; share feelings and uncertainties honestly, without undermining confidence in your core skills.
connect-11: Notice relationship rules you learned early, like never showing weakness, and test new behavior in low-risk settings.
connect-12: If you have less influence, state your wants openly and revisit old agreements so both sides can live with outcomes.
connect-13: Make expectations explicit, raise mismatches early, and frame limits as your own needs so boundaries keep you close.
connect-14: After a serious rupture, approach repair with curiosity about what stopped working rather than blame; relationships can recover stronger.
connect-15: Ask people to change a specific behavior, not their personality, and show them clearly how it affects you.
how-to-know-a-person-01: Make people feel seen by staying curious, asking follow-up questions, and trying to see the world from their side.
how-to-know-a-person-02: Spend unhurried, agenda-free time with people, talking about small things so you can later talk about big ones.
how-to-know-a-person-03: Either give someone your full attention and show it visibly, or switch off deliberately; never half-listen.
how-to-know-a-person-04: Ask the deeper question; people are usually more interested in real conversation and less awkward than you expect.
how-to-know-a-person-05: Ask big, open questions, like what crossroads someone faces, and avoid closed or judging questions that feel like a quiz.
how-to-know-a-person-06: Instead of imagining what someone thinks or feels, ask them directly and listen to the answer.
how-to-know-a-person-07: Paraphrase what someone said and ask if you got it right, letting them correct you until they confirm.
how-to-know-a-person-08: Build on the core of other people's half-formed ideas, help them draw out their thinking, and never top their stories.
how-to-know-a-person-09: Ask how someone came to believe something or who shaped their values, and notice how they frame their story.
how-to-know-a-person-10: With a friend in deep despair, skip advice and cheering up; stay present, acknowledge the pain, and keep reaching out.
how-to-know-a-person-11: Notice the other person's emotion, check your read by asking, then show you care through action.
how-to-know-a-person-12: In hard conversations, build safety before substance, keep the frame they set, and build from what you share.
how-to-know-a-person-13: Understand people through the energy they bring and the life task they face, using these as prompts, not boxes.
how-to-know-a-person-14: Treat your read of anyone, even someone close, as a guess, and keep updating it as you learn more.
humor-seriously-01: Look for what is true, odd, or absurd in everyday moments and share it lightly instead of forcing jokes.
humor-seriously-02: Ask yourself whether your seriousness at work is a real choice or just an assumption about professionalism.
humor-seriously-03: Try light humor; a flat joke costs little, so guard against inappropriate jokes rather than mild unfunniness.
humor-seriously-04: Tease people with more power, never those with less, and never make anyone's identity the punchline.
humor-seriously-05: Joke about your minor flaws, never your competence at the job you are trusted with, especially if your standing is shaky.
humor-seriously-06: Do not joke about a warning, limitation, or request you need taken seriously, because humor makes listeners discount it.
humor-seriously-07: Know your default humor style and your team's, so you can predict where your humor might misfire.
humor-seriously-08: Build humor from a recognizable truth plus a surprise, putting the funny word last and being specific.
humor-seriously-09: Before a risky joke, check whether the bare statement is appropriate, how painful the subject is, and whether you have earned it.
humor-seriously-10: If a joke crosses a line, recognize it, understand why it hurt, and apologize directly without defending your intent.
humor-seriously-11: Share a laugh early in a relationship; it can make the conversation that follows more open and trusting.
humor-seriously-12: Add a small, light line to a negotiation or sales offer; it can build trust and improve the outcome.
humor-seriously-13: Replace autopilot formality in routine messages with small warm touches, choosing clear lightness over sarcasm.
humor-seriously-14: As a leader, make room for humor by laughing at others' jokes, accepting gentle teasing, and building light rituals.
humor-seriously-15: Ask your group for the worst, silliest ideas possible to lower the stakes and surface unusual options worth building on.
humor-seriously-16: Attach a light moment to the point you most want remembered, not to a side detail.
improv-wisdom-01: Treat what others bring you as material to accept and build on, without becoming someone who agrees to everything.
improv-wisdom-02: Prepare your purpose and material, then set the script aside and respond to what is actually happening.
improv-wisdom-03: Do not wait to feel ready; show up and take the next concrete step while still nervous.
improv-wisdom-04: When stuck, start with the most obvious thing in front of you and adjust as you go.
improv-wisdom-05: Aim for an ordinary, adequate contribution rather than brilliance, so you actually contribute and focus on others.
improv-wisdom-06: Put your attention on the other person and surroundings, listening as if you had to repeat it in detail.
improv-wisdom-07: Accept the situation and people as they are, and respond to the conversation you are actually in.
improv-wisdom-08: Ask what your purpose is now, not what you feel like doing, and stay flexible about how to reach it.
improv-wisdom-09: Regularly notice what others have given you, and thank people specifically, including those doing thankless jobs.
improv-wisdom-10: Take risks, and when you slip, acknowledge it lightly, use it if you can, and keep going.
improv-wisdom-11: Focus on making your partners succeed: avoid undermining them, cooperate, and do whatever the moment needs.
improv-wisdom-12: Treat conversations and presentations partly as play, not a test, so you stay flexible and responsive.
improv-wisdom-13: Replace a word-for-word script with a list of questions to yourself, and answer them naturally when speaking.
improv-wisdom-14: When distracting thoughts arise while listening, gently set them aside without self-criticism and return to the person.
made-to-stick-01: Assume your audience lacks your context, and use concrete examples, stories, and outsider tests to check your message.
made-to-stick-02: Diagnose a weak message against simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and story, then strengthen the one or two weakest traits.
made-to-stick-03: Find the single most important point, state it plainly as the goal, and cut everything else, even good points.
made-to-stick-04: Explain a new idea by linking it to something your audience already understands, choosing analogies that guide decisions.
made-to-stick-05: Identify what your audience expects, then break that expectation in a way that makes sense and reinforces your core point.
made-to-stick-06: Before giving facts, raise a question or mystery your audience cares about, show what they do not know, then answer it.
made-to-stick-07: Replace abstract words with concrete details people can see or picture, so your idea is understood, remembered, and shared consistently.
made-to-stick-08: Build credibility inside your message with vivid details, human-scale statistics, one strong proof case, and claims people can test.
made-to-stick-09: To make people care, show one specific person or case before, or instead of, large statistics.
made-to-stick-10: Help people vividly imagine themselves enjoying the benefit, and remember they care about growth and meaning, not just money.
made-to-stick-11: Connect your request to who your audience believes they are, framing it as what someone like them would do.
made-to-stick-12: Collect real stories from daily work and use them to show people how to act and to inspire them.
made-to-stick-13: Give accurate messages emotional and concrete hooks, and be wary of ideas that spread because they grip rather than inform.
made-to-stick-14: Translate big numbers into a familiar comparison people can picture, so they feel the size and act on it.
supercommunicators-01: Notice whether a conversation is about solving a problem, feelings, or identity, and respond in the same layer.
supercommunicators-02: Notice which kind of conversation and mood the other person brings, meet them there, and only later invite a shift.
supercommunicators-03: Notice the conversation type, share goals and ask theirs, exchange feelings, and check whether identities matter to the discussion.
supercommunicators-04: Ask open questions about what others want, state your goals, add options, and match practical or emotional logic to the conversation.
supercommunicators-05: Ask about someone's values, beliefs, or experiences rather than facts, like whether they love their job, not where they work.
supercommunicators-06: Talk less and ask more questions, especially follow-ups; admitting confusion and encouraging others builds shared understanding and liking.
supercommunicators-07: Ask a question, restate the answer in your own words, and check if you got it right until they confirm.
supercommunicators-08: Share how you felt about something first; when the other person reciprocates, trust grows, so do not wait to feel safe.
supercommunicators-09: Read whether someone's mood is positive or negative and their energy high or low, then match both to connect.
supercommunicators-10: When a message threatens someone's identity, stop adding facts; find shared identities, ensure equal footing, and build common groups.
supercommunicators-11: In heated disagreements, aim to understand rather than convert: loop back, acknowledge, find specific agreement, and speak from experience.
supercommunicators-12: Online, be extra polite and grateful, skip sarcasm, and never criticize people publicly, since tone is easily lost.
supercommunicators-13: Build connection together by attending closely to each other, rather than trying to win with a great argument or dominating.
supercommunicators-14: For identity-laden topics, prepare, plan how the talk will happen, name the awkwardness, and speak from your own experience.
talk-wood-brooks-01: When a conversation stalls, check your topics, your questions, your levity, and whether you are prioritizing your partner's needs.
talk-wood-brooks-02: Spend thirty seconds jotting several topics before a conversation, as insurance against lulls and a nudge toward richer subjects.
talk-wood-brooks-03: Use small talk to find better topics, and when pauses grow, climb deeper with a follow-up or switch topics.
talk-wood-brooks-04: Ask more questions than feels natural, especially follow-ups on what the other person just said; it makes you more liked.
talk-wood-brooks-05: Use introductory, mirror, and switch questions in moderation, and lean on follow-up questions to build connection.
talk-wood-brooks-06: If you ask someone a question, follow up on their answer; if you want to share your own story, just share it.
talk-wood-brooks-07: Ask the sensitive question you are avoiding; it costs less than you fear, especially when asked privately with an easy out.
talk-wood-brooks-08: Keep conversations lively with low-risk levity like warmth, laughing at others' humor, and callbacks rather than ambitious jokes.
talk-wood-brooks-09: In disagreements, acknowledge their view, validate feelings, hedge claims, frame positively, and aim to learn rather than win.
talk-wood-brooks-10: Give the sincere compliment or thanks you are holding back, praising choices and efforts rather than appearance.
talk-wood-brooks-11: Watch for fading energy and close a conversation warmly rather than staying too long.
talk-wood-brooks-12: Before a conversation, map your goals and your best guess at your partner's, so you choose more intentionally.
talk-wood-brooks-13: Apologize sincerely for mistakes, commit to change and follow through; even small apologies for things beyond your control build trust.
talk-wood-brooks-14: When a conversation turns hard, ask whether you differ on content, emotions, beliefs, motives, or identity, and address that layer.
think-faster-talk-smarter-01: When put on the spot, calm your nerves, drop perfectionism, see opportunity, listen, give a simple structure, and trim.
think-faster-talk-smarter-02: Manage speaking anxiety with long exhales, slower gestures, a confidence mantra, and repeating your last point when you blank.
think-faster-talk-smarter-03: Before speaking, tell yourself 'I am excited' instead of trying to calm down, keeping the energy but aiming it at opportunity.
think-faster-talk-smarter-04: Aim for connection, not perfection: quiet your inner critic, dare to be obvious, and treat errors as just another take.
think-faster-talk-smarter-05: Treat being put on the spot as a chance to connect rather than a threat, and see tough questions as gifts.
think-faster-talk-smarter-06: Slow down, listen for the content, emotion, and core need beneath the words, and paraphrase it back before answering.
think-faster-talk-smarter-07: Answer on the spot by stating the fact, why it matters to this listener, and the next step.
think-faster-talk-smarter-08: To persuade on the spot, name a problem the listener recognizes, propose a solution, then spell out the benefit.
think-faster-talk-smarter-09: Trim every answer to be precise, relevant to the listener, free of jargon, and short; give the time, not the clock's workings.
think-faster-talk-smarter-10: Give on-the-spot feedback by stating observable facts, their impact on you, an invitation to solve it together, and the implications.
think-faster-talk-smarter-11: In Q&A, paraphrase the question, answer in one sentence, add a concrete example, and explain why it matters to the asker.
think-faster-talk-smarter-12: Name what you did, show you understand its impact, then commit not to repeat it and make any concrete repair.
think-faster-talk-smarter-13: In small talk, be interested rather than interesting: ask setting-specific questions, follow up with 'tell me more', and exit gracefully.
think-faster-talk-smarter-14: For a toast, say why you are gathered, how you are connected, share a short anecdote, then thank the honoree and audience.
think-faster-talk-smarter-15: Pitch on the spot by completing 'What if you could', 'So that', 'For example', and 'And that's not all'.
think-faster-talk-smarter-16: In sudden conflict, pause, listen with curiosity, explore their reasons, acknowledge their view using 'and', then respond strategically.
ames-wazlawek-2014-01: After asserting yourself, do not rush to concede; the other person likely did not see you as overstepping.
ames-wazlawek-2014-02: Ask specific people whether you push too hard or too little, and in which situations, since your own sense is unreliable.
baile-spikes-2000-01: Deliver bad news privately: ask what they know, how much they want, warn, speak plainly, respond to emotion, and plan next steps.
baile-spikes-2000-02: Treat bad news as a series of conversations: share the news first, put key points in writing, and decide later.
bailenson-zoom-fatigue-01: Reduce video call fatigue by shrinking faces, hiding self-view, giving yourself room to move, and using audio when faces add nothing.
berger-catalyst-01: When an idea stalls, ask what is holding people back and remove that specific barrier rather than pushing harder.
berger-catalyst-02: Offer two or three acceptable options and point out gaps between what people want and do, letting them persuade themselves.
berger-catalyst-03: Make the cost of doing nothing visible, such as what the current approach loses monthly, so the status quo stops seeming free.
berger-catalyst-04: Break a big change into small steps within reach, starting with the movable middle and a less contested issue.
berger-catalyst-05: Lower the cost of trying with pilots, samples, trials, or reversible decisions, since experience persuades more than description.
berger-catalyst-06: Bring several independent sources, ideally similar to the listener and close together in time, rather than relying on one advocate.
bitterly-schweitzer-deflection-01: When asked about something you may legitimately keep private, respond with a sincere, relevant question of your own instead of lying.
bodie-2010-01: Identify whether your speaking anxiety comes from your body, thoughts, or lack of skill, and use the matching fix.
bodie-2010-02: Know your opening cold and keep busy beforehand, since nerves peak right before and at the start of a talk.
bond-depaulo-2006-01: Do not trust fidgeting, gaze, or nervousness as signs of lying; acting on such hunches risks wrongly accusing honest people.
bond-depaulo-2006-02: To understand someone, focus on what they say and how they sound compared with usual, and ask follow-ups instead of scanning faces.
boothby-2018-01: Assume a new acquaintance liked you more than you think, and follow up rather than letting self-doubt stop you.
braddock-dillard-2016-01: Use a story to make your point felt and remembered, but back it with evidence and a clear ask.
cialdini-influence-2021-01: Give first, making your help personal, meaningful, and unexpected, and never attach a visible hook to it.
cialdini-influence-2021-02: Honestly tell people that most similar peers already do the desired thing, and never advertise that bad behavior is common.
cialdini-influence-2021-03: Have someone else introduce your expertise before your request, and acknowledge a real weakness, then answer why it matters less.
cialdini-influence-2021-04: Ask for small, voluntary commitments people state or write themselves, like writing their own appointment details, rather than pushing escalation tactics.
cialdini-influence-2021-05: Spend a few minutes finding a genuine point in common before getting to business, especially over email.
cialdini-influence-2021-06: Say what is genuinely unique about your proposal and what they would lose, but only cite real constraints, never invented deadlines.
cialdini-influence-2021-07: When you feel pulled by a favor, crowd, authority, or deadline, pause and check whether the signal is genuine.
cohen-bradford-influence-without-authori: Without authority, treat others as allies, learn their pressures and incentives, and trade what they value for what you need.
Offer what the other person actually values, from meaning to recognition to help, and build goodwill before you need it.
ebrahimi-2019-01: Reduce speaking fear with a deliberate, repeated practice plan combined with challenging your catastrophic predictions, not one-off tips.
feeley-anker-aloe-2012-01: A yes won after retreating from a bigger ask rarely means action, so secure a concrete commitment and follow up.
feinberg-willer-2019-01: Before persuading, learn what the other person values and honestly connect your proposal to those values rather than your own.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-01: In negotiation, ask why the other side wants what they ask for, and look for ways both sides' underlying interests fit.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-02: Be soft on the people and hard on the problem: acknowledge emotions, let them save face, and speak about yourself.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-03: Generate several possible agreements before judging any, trade things each side values differently, and make yes easy for them to defend.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-04: Settle conflicting interests using fair outside standards like market value or precedent, yielding to good reasons but never to pressure.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-05: Before negotiating, work out your best alternative if talks fail, strengthen it, and estimate the other side's alternative too.
fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-06: When attacked in negotiation, do not push back; ask questions, invite criticism, recast attacks onto the problem, and name tricks calmly.
franco-platonic-01: Seek repeated contact with the same people, assume they like you, and take the initiative to follow up.
franco-platonic-02: Raise issues with friends by first saying you value the friendship, then share feelings, ask their view, and own your part.
franco-platonic-03: When a friend's good news stings, say you are happy for them and honestly name that it is hard for you.
gabarro-kotter-managing-your-boss-01: Treat managing your boss as shared work between two fallible people who depend on each other, neither resisting nor passively complying.
gabarro-kotter-managing-your-boss-02: Learn your boss's goals, pressures, and preferred style, like reading versus listening, then adapt your format, timing, and detail.
gabarro-kotter-managing-your-boss-03: Ask your boss what results, timing, and updates they expect, keep them informed including bad news, and use their time selectively.
gable-2004-01: When someone shares good news, respond with genuine enthusiasm and questions that help them relive it, not a muted 'that's nice'.
gable-2004-02: Tell people about your good news, not just your troubles; sharing it amplifies the good feeling and strengthens relationships.
giurge-bohns-2021-01: When sending non-urgent emails, especially after hours, say when you need a reply; when receiving them, assume they can wait.
givi-kirk-2024-01: Feel free to occasionally decline a casual invitation considerately; it hurts the inviter far less than you expect.
gottman-seven-principles-01: In conflict, replace criticism with a gentle complaint, contempt with appreciation, defensiveness with responsibility, and stonewalling with a calming break.
gottman-seven-principles-02: Notice and engage with small bids for attention, like a shared story or sigh, instead of missing or ignoring them.
gottman-seven-principles-03: When an argument overwhelms you, say so, take at least twenty minutes doing something calming, then return to the conversation.
gottman-seven-principles-04: Build everyday goodwill through small, frequent appreciation and affection, so your repair attempts land during conflict.
gottman-seven-principles-05: For recurring conflicts rooted in lasting differences, keep a friendly ongoing dialogue and explore the deeper meaning behind each position.
guyer-vocal-confidence-01: Land key statements with falling intonation and an energetic pace, but do not rely on delivery to rescue weak content.
hall-2019-01: Invest many leisure hours in a few chosen people, moving time together from obligation, like work, to relaxed activities.
hall-nonverbal-2019-01: Treat any single body-language cue as a question to check, not an answer about what someone feels or thinks.
high-dillard-2012-01: When comforting someone, explicitly acknowledge their feelings, help them put them into words, and treat them as understandable, not minimized.
jamieson-2018-01: Before a high-stakes moment, read your racing heart as your body fueling you to perform, rather than trying to calm down.
kalla-broockman-2020-01: On charged topics, ask about the other person's experience, listen without judging, and share your own story instead of more arguments.
keysar-henly-2002-01: When accuracy matters, ask listeners to say back in their own words what they took away, rather than trusting a nod.
king-social-chemistry-01: Notice whether you tend toward large, bridging, or tight-knit networks, and strengthen the ties you already have before adding names.
king-social-chemistry-02: Approach networking by thinking about what you can offer, and start by doing something generous or asking for small help.
kluger-listening-2024-01: Spend more of your conversations listening; it reliably builds trust and relationships with little downside.
kluger-listening-2024-02: When someone is dug in, invite them to talk it through and listen fully before offering your counterpoints.
kross-2014-01: Before a stressful moment, coach yourself using your own name or 'you' instead of 'I', as you would a friend.
kruger-epley-2005-01: Reread important messages in a flat or opposite tone, and move sarcasm, criticism, or loaded content to voice when misreading costs.
kruger-epley-2005-02: Treat your first read of a curt or ambiguous message as a hypothesis, consider a kinder reading, and ask before reacting.
levin-dormant-ties-2011-01: Reach out to contacts you have not spoken with in years; they offer fresh ideas and still trust you.
lewicki-apologies-2016-01: In an apology, plainly accept responsibility first and offer to repair the damage; asking for forgiveness matters least.
liu-2023-01: Send a brief, unprompted check-in to someone you have lost touch with; it lands better than you expect.
mesmer-magnus-2012-01: Use humor as a pressure valve aimed at the situation or yourself, never at colleagues.
miller-rollnick-mi-2023-01: Instead of supplying reasons to change, ask questions that draw out the person's own reasons, and reflect them back.
miller-rollnick-mi-2023-02: Before advising, ask what they know and if they want input, offer it briefly, then ask what they make of it.
miller-rollnick-mi-2023-03: When someone pushes back, reflect both sides of their ambivalence and say the decision is theirs, rather than arguing harder.
minto-pyramid-principle-01: Lead with your answer as a full assertion, then group distinct, non-overlapping supporting points in a deliberate order beneath it.
minto-pyramid-principle-02: Open with the familiar situation, what has changed, and the question that raises, then give your answer.
minto-pyramid-principle-03: If your conclusion is unclear, group your points and summarize each group to find it, then write answer first.
morrison-2014-voice-01: Speak up to someone who can act, with a concrete next step; as a leader, show you will act and protect speakers.
morrison-2014-voice-02: Notice unspoken rules that keep you silent, like needing a solution first, and test them against the actual situation.
morrison-2014-voice-03: Raise concerns early and privately, with evidence and a proposed next step, making your constructive intent and shared goal explicit.
mroz-allen-2018-meetings-01: Meet only when discussion is needed, set goals and an agenda, invite all voices, and send decisions, owners, and deadlines afterward.
mroz-allen-2018-meetings-02: When meetings slide into general complaining, welcome specific problems but steer quickly back to what the group can act on.
overall-mcnulty-2017-01: Be clearly direct about serious, fixable problems, and lead with warmth for minor or unchangeable issues or a fragile partner.
overall-mcnulty-2017-02: Instead of guilt trips or sulking, ask directly for reassurance if you need it and for the specific change you want.
rafaeli-gleason-2009-01: Before helping, check what kind of support is wanted and when, protect their sense of competence, and keep support two-way.
rafaeli-gleason-2009-02: Give open, explicit comfort when someone is visibly upset; when they are coping, help quietly so they feel competent.
rajkumar-weak-ties-2022-01: In a job search, reach beyond close friends to people you know a little who move in partly different circles.
riedl-2021-01: Improve how your team coordinates and notices each other, such as who gets heard, rather than just recruiting another star.
rogelberg-meetings-01: As a meeting leader, act as a steward of others' time and ask attendees directly how your meetings are working.
rogelberg-meetings-02: Phrase each agenda item as a question the group must answer; if you cannot find one, skip the meeting.
rogelberg-meetings-03: Invite the smallest group that can do the work, use a timed agenda, and let others opt out with input and notes.
rogelberg-meetings-04: Estimate how long your agenda needs, trim five to ten minutes, and consider standing or walking meetings.
rogelberg-meetings-05: Have people write ideas silently and individually first, then pool and discuss them, so no one anchors on the loudest voice.
rogelberg-meetings-06: Host your meetings: greet and thank people, introduce strangers, start on time, and actively bring quieter people in on calls.
rogers-busy-readers-01: Assume readers give your message a small attention budget, and make the important content easy to find within it.
rogers-busy-readers-02: Cut whole ideas, not just words, since your instinct favors too long, and move extra detail below the sign-off.
rogers-busy-readers-03: Make one request per message, and make it quick to answer with yes or no questions or numbered options.
rogers-busy-readers-04: Use headings and short bullets to help skimmers, and apply one consistent emphasis style only to the single most important thing.
rogers-busy-readers-05: Lead with the part your reader values most, and say plainly who the message is for and why it matters.
rogers-norton-artful-dodger-01: Rehearse answers to expected hard questions so you sound fluent, and briefly restate each question before answering it.
rogers-norton-artful-dodger-02: Write down the exact question, then check the answer against it before deciding whether you actually got one.
savitsky-gilovich-2003-01: Remind yourself before speaking that the audience sees only a fraction of the nervousness you feel inside.
schneider-2018-signaling-01: When explaining complex material, pick the few essential pieces and make them visibly stand out, avoiding distracting effects like flashing.
shockley-camera-fatigue-01: Make cameras optional in recurring meetings, ask for them only where faces add value, and do not assume camera-off means disengaged.
thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-01: Do not assume the other side wants the opposite on every issue; ask about priorities and check for shared interests.
thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-02: If well informed, open with an ambitious but justifiable offer; if they anchor first, recall your own target and alternatives.
thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-03: Negotiate several issues together and offer multiple equally good packages, so their choice reveals their priorities.
thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-04: When sides disagree about the future, tie terms to measurable outcomes so each gets what it believes will happen.
ury-positive-no-01: Say no by naming the interest you are protecting, declining plainly, then proposing an alternative the other person can accept.
ury-positive-no-02: Notice whether you tend to give in, snap, or avoid when refusing, and practice protecting both your interest and the relationship.
van-laer-2014-01: Tell stories with a specific character people can empathize with, concrete events they can picture, and situations that feel believable.
